The Little Lantern

Once there was a small lantern that hung by the door of an old barn. Every evening the farmer lit it, and every evening the lantern glowed a warm yellow. The moths loved it. The mice did not, because they liked the dark. One windy night the lantern flickered and almost went out. A tiny moth landed on its glass and said, "Don't give up. I will stay with you." The wind blew harder, but the moth spread its wings like a little shield, and the flame grew steady again. In the morning the farmer found the lantern still burning and a very sleepy moth curled up beside it.

Mia and the Red Kite

Mia had a red kite with a long blue tail. She took it to the top of the hill every Saturday. The first time she tried to fly it, the kite spun in circles and fell into a bush. The second time it tangled with a tree. Mia sat down and felt sad. Her grandfather came over and sat beside her. "A kite needs wind and patience," he said. "You have the wind. Now wait for the right moment." So Mia waited, and when a long, soft breeze came over the hill, she let out the string a little at a time. The red kite climbed higher and higher until it was a tiny dot against the clouds. Mia laughed so loudly that the sheep looked up from their grass.

The Fox Who Wanted a Hat

A young fox saw a traveler walking down the road with a bright green hat. "I want one just like that," thought the fox. He asked the rabbit, who knew about gardens. He asked the owl, who knew about the night. He asked the old turtle, who knew about almost everything. The turtle said, "Hats are made by people, and people trade for them. What can you offer?" The fox thought for a long time. Then he remembered that he was very good at finding the sweetest berries in the forest. He gathered a basket of them and carried it to the village. A kind woman at the market looked at the berries, smiled, and handed him a small hat made of woven grass. It was not green, but it fit perfectly, and the fox wore it proudly all summer.

The Clock That Ran Backwards

In a quiet town there was a clock tower with a clock that ran backwards. Nobody knew why. The mayor wanted to fix it, but the clockmaker said, "Wait and see." On the first day of spring, a girl named Ana noticed something odd. When she looked at the clock, she always remembered something nice from the past: a picnic, a song, a birthday cake with too many candles. She told her friends, and soon the whole town agreed. The backwards clock reminded them of good things. The mayor decided to leave it alone, and the clockmaker winked.

Pip the Penguin Learns to Slide

Pip was a penguin who was afraid of the ice slide. All his friends zoomed down it with a whoosh and a splash. Pip stood at the top and shivered. "What if I fall?" he asked. "Then you get up," said his friend Lola. "That is how everybody learns." Pip took a deep breath, closed his eyes, and pushed off with his flippers. Down he went, faster and faster, and landed in the snow with a soft thump. For a moment he lay very still. Then he opened his eyes and began to giggle. "Again!" he cried. He climbed back up and slid all afternoon.

The Bakery on Maple Street

Every morning, before the sun came up, Mr. Okafor opened his little bakery on Maple Street. The smell of warm bread drifted down the block and woke the neighbors one by one. Children stopped by on the way to school for a cinnamon roll. Workers stopped for coffee and a piece of rye. One rainy day a stray dog wandered in and sat beside the oven, dripping. Mr. Okafor did not shoo him away. He gave the dog a bowl of water and a crust of bread. The next morning the dog was waiting at the door, and the morning after that too. Soon the whole street knew him as Biscuit, the bakery dog, and he greeted every customer with a wag of his tail.

The Moon's Lost Sock

One night the moon looked down and saw that she had lost a sock. "It must have fallen somewhere," she said. The stars helped her search. They looked behind the clouds and under the northern lights. A comet zipped by and said it had seen something fuzzy near the planet Saturn. Sure enough, there was the sock, wrapped around one of the rings like a scarf. The moon laughed and pulled it back on. The next time you see the moon looking a bit crooked, you will know that she is probably just fixing her socks.

Tomas and the Giant Pumpkin

Tomas planted one small seed in the corner of the garden. He watered it every morning and talked to it every evening, mostly about his day at school. By midsummer a green vine had crawled across the whole yard, and in the middle of it sat a pumpkin as big as a wheelbarrow. The neighbors came to look. A reporter from the town paper took a picture. Tomas was proud, but when autumn came he did something surprising. He cut the pumpkin open and shared it with everyone on the street. There was pumpkin soup, pumpkin bread, and roasted pumpkin seeds for the birds. "It tastes better when it is shared," said Tomas.

The Sleepy Bear and the Busy Bees

A bear woke up too early in the winter and could not go back to sleep. He wandered through the snowy forest until he heard a soft humming from a hollow tree. Inside, a colony of bees was keeping warm in a tight, buzzing ball. The queen invited the bear to sit by the opening. "You may stay until spring," she said, "if you promise not to eat our honey." The bear promised. He sat in the doorway of the tree and listened to the humming until his eyes grew heavy. When he woke again, the snow had melted, the flowers were blooming, and the bees gave him a small taste of honey as a thank-you for keeping watch.

Nora's Paper Boat

After the big storm, a stream ran through the park. Nora folded a boat from a sheet of newspaper and set it on the water. It bobbed past the swings, spun around a rock, and slipped under the little bridge. Nora ran along the bank to keep up. A duck paddled beside the boat for a while, as if escorting it. At the end of the stream, where the water spilled into a pond, the boat finally slowed and floated to a stop. Nora scooped it out, dried it on her sleeve, and carried it home. She decided that every boat deserves a long journey and a safe landing.

The Robot Who Learned to Whistle

A small robot named Bolt worked in a toy factory, tightening screws all day long. He was good at his job, but he wished he could make music. The workers hummed while they worked, and Bolt could only click and whir. One lunch break a girl named Priya showed him how to shape his mouth and blow gently. Bolt tried, and out came a thin, wobbly sound, like a kettle just beginning to boil. He practiced every day. By winter he could whistle a whole song, and the workers asked for it each morning. Bolt still tightened screws all day, but now he did it in time with the tune.

The Island of Lost Umbrellas

Far out at sea there is a tiny island where all the lost umbrellas end up. The wind carries them there from every city in the world. Black ones, yellow ones, ones with polka dots and ones with a broken rib. A crab named Clem looks after them. He opens them one by one and lines them up along the beach so they can dry in the sun. When it rains, the whole island looks like a field of colorful mushrooms. Clem sits under the biggest umbrella and listens to the drops, quite certain that he has the best job in the ocean.

Grandma's Quilt

Grandma kept a quilt on the end of her bed, stitched from scraps of old clothes. There was a square from Dad's first shirt, a square from Aunt Rosa's curtains, and a square from a dress Grandma wore to a dance when she was seventeen. When Lily was sick with a cold, Grandma wrapped her in the quilt and told the story behind every square. By the time she reached the last one, a patch of faded blue denim, Lily was fast asleep and her cheeks were warm. The next morning her cold was gone, and Lily was sure the quilt had done it.

Two Snails and a Race

Two snails, Sam and Dot, decided to race across the garden path. They lined up at a crack in the stone and counted to three, very slowly. Sam went straight ahead, but a leaf stood in his way, and he spent an hour going around it. Dot took the long way beside the wall, stopping now and then to eat a bit of lettuce. At sunset they met at the finish line, which was a daisy. Neither could say who had won. "Let's call it a tie," said Sam. "And a snack," said Dot, and they shared the daisy's shade until the stars came out.

The Boy Who Counted Clouds

Ben liked to lie on his back in the grass and count clouds. One afternoon he counted twelve. The next day there were only three. On the third day the sky was empty and blue, and Ben felt a little disappointed. But then he noticed a thin white streak far above him, left by an airplane, and he realized that even an empty sky had something to count. He started keeping a notebook of everything he saw overhead: birds, kites, jets, a balloon, and once, a feather drifting down all on its own. His notebook grew thick, and his teacher asked to read it aloud to the whole class.

The Dragon With the Cold

A small dragon named Ember woke up with a terrible cold. Instead of fire, she could only produce little puffs of smoke and a very loud sneeze. The knights in the nearby castle laughed, but the cook felt sorry for her and sent over a pot of hot chicken soup. Ember drank it all and slept for two days. When she woke, she breathed out a perfect, bright orange flame and used it to toast a whole tray of marshmallows for the village fair. The knights admitted that maybe dragons were not so scary, and they asked for seconds.

The Night Market

When the sun went down, the night market came alive. Lanterns were strung between the stalls, and the air filled with the smell of grilled corn and sweet rice. An old man sold paper birds that really flapped their wings when you pulled the string. A woman sold jars of fireflies for exactly one hour, after which she let them all go. Children ran from stall to stall with coins clenched in their hands. Little Sun bought a single paper bird and held it up high as she walked home, and for a moment it seemed to fly.
